issues.legal_issue: A party may not introduce an appellate ground that depends on factual matters when those matters were not pleaded and would require evidence or factual inquiry.
material_facts: The appellant did not refer to the nationalisation legislation in its written statement, and no issue or argument on its effect was raised before the trial court, appellate court, or revisional court.

The appellant sought to raise the point for the first time before the Supreme Court without amending its pleadings; its claim that it acted as the Central Government’s agent depended on facts that had not been pleaded or proved.
issues.conclusion: The appellant could not rely on the unpleaded, fact-dependent agency ground; a new ground involving a pure question of law that requires no inquiry or proof may be raised at any stage.
issues.legal_principle: Relief should ordinarily not be granted on a ground outside the pleadings, and evidence cannot be relied on where it is not supported by pleadings. Material facts must be pleaded and proved, and a matter should not ordinarily be decided without an issue having been framed. A new pure legal ground requiring no inquiry or proof may be raised at any stage, but a new factual case requires amendment of the pleadings. The Court relied on M/s. Trojan & Co. v. R.M.N.N. Nagappa Chettiar, State of Maharashtra v. Hindustan Construction Company Ltd., Kalyan Singh Chouhan v. C.P. Joshi, Ram Sarup Gupta v. Bishun Narain Inter College, Bachhaj Nahar v. Nilima Mandal, Kashi Nath v. Jaganath, Biswanath Agarwalla v. Sabitri Bera, Syed and Company v. State of Jammu & Kashmir, Chinta Lingam v. Government of India, J. Jermons v. Aliammal, M/s. Sanghvi Reconditioners Pvt. Ltd. v. Union of India, and Greater Mohali Area Development Authority v. Manju Jain; it also referred to Order XIV and Order VIII Rule 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

predicates.appellate_proceeding: A party seeks to advance a ground in an appeal or other appellate proceeding.
predicates.new_ground_requires_factual_inquiry: The proposed ground depends on factual matters that would require evidence or factual inquiry.
predicates.factual_basis_not_pleaded: The party did not set out the material factual basis for the ground in its pleadings.

issues.definition: When a party seeks to advance a fact-dependent ground in an appellate proceeding without having pleaded its factual basis, that new factual ground is not permitted.

issues.legal_issue: A government company that is a distinct legal entity and falls within a category excluded from rent-control protection is not exempt from rent-control law as the government, a government department, or its agent.
material_facts: The appellant was a government company, distinct from the Central Government, and its rights were controlled by the nationalisation legislation rather than by the Central Government.
The appellant claimed that the Central Government remained the tenant and that the appellant held the premises as its agent.
The respondents sought eviction of the appellant, and the appellant claimed protection under the rent-control law’s exemption for premises let to the Government.
The appellant fell within the categories of entities excluded from rent-control protection under the applicable law.
issues.conclusion: The appellant was not the Government or a government department, could not claim to be the Government’s agent, and was not entitled to exemption under either of the relevant rent-control exemptions.
issues.legal_principle: The meaning of “Government” depends on the statutory context. A government company remains legally distinct from the Government, even where the Government owns its shares or controls it; an instrumentality or agency of the State for constitutional purposes is not necessarily an agent under Section 182 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872. An agent does not acquire independent rights in property held for its principal, but the appellant’s rights had vested in it and it was not an agent of the Central Government. Section 230 of the Contract Act concerns an agent’s liability where a principal is disclosed. Section 3(1)(a) and (b) of the Maharashtra Rent Control Act, 1999 excludes specified categories of tenants from protection. The Court relied on State of Punjab v. Raja Ram, Food Corporation of India v. Municipal Committee, Jalalabad, A.K. Bindal v. Union of India, Sukhdev Singh v. Bhagatram Sardar Singh Raghuvanshi, Ramana Dayaram Shetty v. International Airport Authority of India, Federal Bank v. Sagar Thomas, Southern Roadways Ltd. v. S.M. Krishnan, Prem Nath Motors Ltd. v. Anurag Mittal, and Saraswat Coop. Bank Ltd. v. State of Maharashtra. It applied Leelabai Gajanan Pansare v. Oriental Insurance Company Ltd., which held that the excluded categories are capable of paying market rent, and also referred to D.C. Bhatia v. Union of India.

rule.if: rent_control_eviction_case and tenant_is_government_company and tenant_is_distinct_from_government and tenant_falls_within_excluded_category

predicates.rent_control_eviction_case: A landlord seeks eviction of a tenant in a proceeding governed by rent-control law.
predicates.tenant_is_government_company: The tenant is a company established or owned by the government rather than a government department.
predicates.tenant_is_distinct_from_government: The company has a legal identity and rights distinct from the government.
predicates.tenant_falls_within_excluded_category: The tenant belongs to a category that the applicable rent-control law excludes from its protection.

issues.definition: In a rent-control eviction proceeding, a distinct government company within an excluded tenant category is not exempt from rent-control law.

issues.legal_issue: When a statutory scheme transfers a textile undertaking’s rights first to the Central Government and then immediately to a corporation, the undertaking’s existing tenancy interest vests in the corporation, not in the Government as its agent.
material_facts: The lease of the premises to the textile mill had expired, and the mill continued as a tenant holding over.
The premises’ owners had leased the premises to the mill; they did not own the textile undertaking.
The mill had only a tenancy interest in the premises.
The statutory scheme transferred the textile undertaking’s rights and interests to the Central Government and required them to vest immediately thereafter in the appellant corporation.
The appellant claimed that it held the tenancy as the Central Government’s agent, but the rights had vested in the appellant as a separate legal entity.
issues.conclusion: Only the textile undertaking’s existing tenancy interest, and not the premises owners’ interest, vested through the Central Government and then in the appellant; the appellant could not characterize that vesting as holding the tenancy merely as the Government’s agent.
issues.legal_principle: The meaning of “vest” depends on the statutory context and may refer to vesting of title, possession, or a limited interest. The relevant nationalisation law transferred the rights, title, and interest of the textile undertaking to the Central Government and immediately thereafter to the National Textile Corporation; the undertaking’s tenancy interest was the relevant interest because the premises’ owners were not owners of the textile undertaking. The Court referred to the definitions of “owner” and “textile undertaking” in Sections 2(g) and 2(m), the transfer provisions in Sections 3(1) and 3(2), and Section 4(6) concerning pending proceedings. It relied on Fruit & Vegetable Merchants Union v. Delhi Improvement Trust, Maharaj Singh v. State of Uttar Pradesh, Municipal Corporation of Hyderabad v. P.N. Murthy, Vatticherukuru Village Panchayat v. Nori Venkatarama Deekshithulu, Dr. M. Ismail Faruqui v. Union of India, Government of A.P. v. H.E.H. The Nizam, K.V. Shivakumar v. Appropriate Authority, Municipal Corporation of Greater Bombay v. Hindustan Petroleum Corporation, and Sulochana Chandrakant Galande v. Pune Municipal Transport.

predicates.statutory_transfer_case: A proceeding concerns the statutory transfer of the rights and interests of an undertaking.
predicates.undertaking_had_only_tenancy_interest: The undertaking held a tenancy interest in the premises, while the premises were owned by another person.
predicates.law_requires_immediate_transfer_of_acqui: The governing law requires rights first transferred to the government to be transferred immediately thereafter to a corporation.

issues.definition: Where an undertaking has only a tenancy interest and the governing law requires immediate transfer of acquired rights to a corporation, that tenancy interest vests in the corporation rather than remaining with the government.
